claim.pdf_says: 14.9.37.4   General rules  — printed in the same bold heading style as 14.9.37.1/.2/.3, i.e. a fourth-level subsection of 14.9.37 SEARCH statement.
claim.markdown_says: specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 30519: "## 14.9.37.4 General rules" — H2, the same level as "## 14.9.37 SEARCH statement" (line 30404), while sibling subsections 14.9.37.1 and 14.9.37.2 are H3.
claim.why_it_matters: Same defect as 14.9.37.3: the General rules for SEARCH — the longest and most heavily cited part of the clause (GR 1 through GR 9, pp.722-725) — are detached from 14.9.37 in the document outline and read as an independent top-level section. Cross-references of the form "14.9.37.4, General rules" resolve to a node that is not nested under SEARCH.

verdict.reasoning:
CONFIRMED as a genuine PDF-vs-markdown structural discrepancy, though the claim's label and its stated rationale are both wrong.

What I verified independently:

1. PDF page 752 (printed page 722), rendered at 300 dpi: the heading reads "14.9.37.4   General rules", bold, flush left, immediately after syntax rule 13 and immediately before "ALL FORMATS" and GR 1. Text confirmed verbatim.

2. Markdown levels confirmed by direct read (line numbers are off by 3 from the claim — see corrections): line 30407 "## 14.9.37 SEARCH statement"; 30410 "### 14.9.37.1 General"; 30415 "### 14.9.37.2 General formats"; 30476 "## 14.9.37.3 Syntax rules"; 30522 "## 14.9.37.4 General rules". So .4 sits at the SAME markdown depth as its own parent 14.9.37, while its siblings .1 and .2 are one level deeper.

3. My first refutation attempt FAILED, and it is worth recording why, because it defeats the claim's own stated evidence. I rendered page 750 to test the claim's typography argument. On page 750 the PDF prints "14.9.37 SEARCH statement", "14.9.37.1 General" and "14.9.37.2 General formats" in the SAME bold face and SAME size. The parent and its children are typographically indistinguishable. Therefore "printed in the same bold heading style as 14.9.37.1/.2/.3" proves nothing about level — 14.9.37 itself shares that style. Had typography been the only evidence, I would have rejected this as an unprovable formatting preference.

4. The claim survives on evidence it did not cite. The PDF carries an explicit 2090-entry bookmark outline, and it assigns levels unambiguously:
     level 3  '14.9.37 SEARCH statement'      p.750
     level 4  '14.9.37.1 General'             p.750
     level 4  '14.9.37.2 General formats'     p.750
     level 4  '14.9.37.3 Syntax rules'        p.751
     level 4  '14.9.37.4 General rules'       p.752
   The canonical source therefore states outright that 14.9.37.4 is a child of 14.9.37, not its peer. The markdown encodes both as "##". That is a contradiction of the PDF's own structure, not a transcription style choice, so it is in scope for this reconciliation — whose driving script names "a heading demoted to bold" as one of the four artefacts that caused rule-catalog extractor bugs.

5. The markdown's own mapping is PDF level 3 -> H2, PDF level 4 -> H3, and it is applied correctly to the immediate neighbours: 14.9.36 is H2 with 14.9.36.1/.2/.3/.4 all H3; 14.9.35 likewise; 14.9.38.1/.2/.3 are H3. Document-wide, four-part headings are H3 620 times versus H2 162 times. So H3 is both the correct mapping and the dominant convention, and 14.9.37.3/.4 are sporadic breaks from it — not a deliberate rule.

What does NOT hold up: nothing is missing (the heading is present verbatim, so "missing-heading" mislabels it), no prose is lost, and the cross-reference rationale is factually false — see corrected_description.
verdict.corrected_description: REAL, but re-describe it as follows. Correct kind: wrong-heading-level, NOT missing-heading. The heading text "14.9.37.4 General rules" is present verbatim in the markdown at line 30522, preceded by its correct anchor . No text, no rule, and no meaning is lost. The defect is purely that it is emitted as H2 ("##") where the transcription's own convention and the PDF's own outline both require H3 ("###"). Correct line numbers: the heading is at line 30522, not 30519; "## 14.9.37 SEARCH statement" is at line 30407, not 30404. The claim is uniformly 3 lines low, suggesting it was authored against a slightly different revision of the file. Correct evidence: drop the typography argument. The PDF prints 14.9.37 (a level-3 heading) in the same bold face and size as 14.9.37.1/.2/.4, so heading style carries no level information in this document. The decisive evidence is the PDF's embedded bookmark outline, which explicitly tags '14.9.37 SEARCH statement' as level 3 and '14.9.37.1' through '14.9.37.4' as level 4. Correct impact: the stated cross-reference harm does not exist. The string "14.9.37.4" occurs exactly ONCE in the entire markdown — the heading itself — and the document contains ZERO cross-references of the form "N.N.N.N, General rules". The spec cites these rules as "(14.9.37, SEARCH statement, General rule 9)", which resolves correctly and is unaffected. The real harm is confined to structure-consuming tooling: any TOC builder, outline walker, or rule-catalog extractor that infers parentage from heading depth will attribute SEARCH's GR 1-9 to a top-level section instead of to 14.9.37, which is precisely the extractor-bug class this reconciliation was commissioned to fix. Scope note for the ledger: this is not isolated to SEARCH. 14.9.37.3 (line 30476) has the identical defect, as do 14.9.38.4 (30685), 14.9.39.3 (30949) and 14.9.39.4 (31160); document-wide 162 four-part headings are H2 against 620 correctly at H3. Treat this as one instance of a recurring level-demotion class and fix it with a single sweep keyed on heading-number depth, rather than as a page-752 one-off. Fix: change line 30522 from "## 14.9.37.4 General rules" to "### 14.9.37.4 General rules".
